question: Let a circle be centered at a lattice point in the plane and have radius \(\sqrt{n}\) where \(n\) is a positive integer. A lattice point is a point whose two coordinates are both integers. The circle is said to *pass through* a lattice point if the point lies exactly on the circle (its distance from the centre equals the radius). Find the sum of all positive integers \(n<500\) for which there exists such a circle that passes through exactly 12 lattice points.
why_omitted: Many solvers only consider factors of 2 when forming the multiplier m, forgetting that a square of a prime ≡3 (mod 4) such as 3² may also be multiplied without changing the number of lattice points on the circle.
solution:
Let the centre of the circle be the origin; translating the whole picture does not change the number of lattice points on the circle.  The lattice points on the circle \(x^{2}+y^{2}=n\) correspond exactly to integer solutions of the Diophantine equation \(x^{2}+y^{2}=n\).  The well‑known formula for the number of representations of \(n\) as a sum of two squares (counting order and signs) is
\[r_{2}(n)=\begin{cases}0,&\text{if some prime }p\equiv3\pmod4\text{ occurs to an odd power in }n,\\[4pt]
4\displaystyle\prod_{p\equiv1\,(4)}(e_{p}+1),&\text{otherwise},\end{cases}\]
where \(e_{p}\) is the exponent of the prime \(p\equiv1\pmod4\) in the factorisation of \(n\).  The circle therefore passes through exactly \(r_{2}(n)\) lattice points.
We want \(r_{2}(n)=12\).  Hence
\[4\prod_{p\equiv1\,(4)}(e_{p}+1)=12\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\prod_{p\equiv1\,(4)}(e_{p}+1)=3.
\]
The only way a product of positive integers can be 3 is to have a single factor equal to 3 and no other factors.  Thus there is exactly one prime \(p\equiv1\pmod4\) occurring in \(n\) and its exponent must satisfy \(e_{p}+1=3\), i.e. \(e_{p}=2\).  Consequently
\[n=p^{2}\cdot m,\]
where \(p\) is a prime congruent to 1 mod 4, and \(m\) is any integer whose prime factors are either 2 or primes \(q\equiv3\pmod4\), each occurring to an even exponent (so that they do not affect \(r_{2}\)).
We are asked for \(n<500\).  The squares of the relevant primes are
\[5^{2}=25,\;13^{2}=169,\;17^{2}=289,\;29^{2}=841>500,\]
so only \(p=5,13,17\) need be considered.

*For \(p=5\) (\(p^{2}=25\)).*  The possible multipliers \(m\) (made from 2‑powers and even powers of primes \(\equiv3\pmod4\)) that keep the product below 500 are
\[1,\;2,\;2^{2}=4,\;2^{3}=8,\;2^{4}=16,\;3^{2}=9,\;2\cdot3^{2}=18.\]
Multiplying by 25 gives the seven admissible values
\[25,\;50,\;100,\;200,\;400,\;225,\;450.\]

*For \(p=13\) (\(p^{2}=169\)).*  Multipliers \(m\) allowed are \(1\) and \(2\), producing
\[169,\;338.\]

*For \(p=17\) (\(p^{2}=289\)).*  Only \(m=1\) works, giving \(289\).

Collecting all distinct \(n<500\) we obtain the ten numbers
\[25,\;50,\;100,\;200,\;400,\;225,\;450,\;169,\;338,\;289.\]
Each of them indeed yields \(r_{2}(n)=12\) lattice points on the corresponding circle, and no other integer \(n<500\) does.
The required sum is therefore
\[25+50+100+200+400+225+450+169+338+289=2246.\]
Hence the answer is **2246**.
